logline: The Roy family - owners of a global media empire - tear each other apart in the long shadow of a patriarch who refuses to die or to let anyone else truly live.

renewal.note: Concluded after 4 seasons on May 28, 2023; the finale was one of HBO's most-watched drama episodes ever.

bollymeter.basis: 89% RT - modest by Succession standards, but the essential table-setting. The show's toxic family grammar needs S1 to make the later seasons land. IMDb audience 8.1/10.

pull_quotes.text: A wickedly funny, ruthlessly observed portrait of ultra-wealth that bristles with dark energy and exceptional performances.

seasons.review_body: Succession S1 arrived to modest critical fanfare - 89% RT, respectable but not deafening - and then word of mouth turned it into the decade's prestige obsession. Jesse Armstrong's pilot establishes the Roy family as a comedy of cruelty: Logan (Brian Cox) summons his children to assess their fitness for succession, and the verdict is quietly damning of all of them. The humour is Shakespearean in its mode - characters funny because they are awful and awful because they want things they cannot name. Cox and Jeremy Strong (Kendall) anchor the patriarch-son tension that powers the whole series. Critics noted the show was funnier and meaner than expected from a HBO drama. The slow build here is essential: the show is mapping the psychic damage of extreme wealth, and it cannot rush that cartography.

bollymeter.basis: 97% RT. The season that converted the mainstream: Kendall's arc, Boar on the Floor, the yacht finale. Audiences and critics aligned on this as a genuine leap into greatness. IMDb 8.6/10.

pull_quotes.text: Succession Season 2 is a triumph - funnier, darker, and more emotionally devastating than its acclaimed first year.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 is where Succession became a cultural phenomenon rather than a prestige recommendation. The show found its full register: blackly comedic, genuinely devastating, capable of 'Boar on the Floor' and the Season 2 finale within the same run. Kieran Culkin's Roman and Sarah Snook's Shiv get the space to become fully articulated Roy disasters. The ATN / Waystar Cruises corruption arc gives the show corporate thriller propulsion, but the real engine is still the father-shaped void each child is drowning in. The finale - Kendall's press conference - is one of the great HBO season endings. Critics pushed the score to 97%. The show went from 'very good HBO' to 'all-time' conversation in a single season.
seasons.season_over_season: A definitive leap: darker, funnier, and more structurally assured. The ensemble is now operating as a unit and the finale is the first of the show's knockout punches.

bollymeter.basis: 97% RT. The legal-and-family fallout from S2's detonation. The Italian villa finale remains one of the most discussed HBO episodes in years. IMDb 8.7/10.

pull_quotes.text: Season 3 maintains Succession's position at the peak of prestige television - ruthlessly written, unforgettably performed.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 is where the fan base fractured slightly - some found the middle episodes treading water - but critics held at 97% because the writing and performance level never actually dropped. The Kendall-vs-Logan war enters its most explicitly political phase; the Waystar board maneuvres involve real-world media mogul allegory that sharpens in retrospect. The Italy finale is a masterclass in structural betrayal: the show builds apparent hope and then demolishes it from an unexpected direction. Logan's reveal about the family trust rewrites the season's entire emotional architecture in its final act. Matthew Macfadyen's Tom Wambsgans acquires genuine menace here for the first time - a development that pays enormous dividends in S4.
seasons.season_over_season: Slightly leaner momentum mid-season, but the finale is the show's most ruthless act of structural surprise yet.

bollymeter.basis: 97% RT, IMDb 8.8/10. The final season navigates Logan's death with extraordinary craft; 'Connor's Wedding' is cited as one of the best individual episodes in recent HBO history. The finale divides audiences but not critics.

pull_quotes.text: A final season of remarkable assurance - Succession ends exactly as it lived, with cruelty, wit, and genuine heartbreak.

seasons.review_body: Season 4 is the rarest thing: a final season that lives up to what came before. Logan Roy's death - arriving in episode 3, mid-season, without warning - restructures the remaining seven episodes into the grief story the show was always secretly telling. 'Connor's Wedding' handles the death with such real-time emotional devastation that it became one of the most discussed prestige TV episodes of the 2020s. The siblings' attempts to fill the vacuum are funny and horrible in equal measure. The finale - electing a successor who is neither Roy child - is divisive among audiences but near-unanimously praised by critics as the only honest conclusion available to the premise. Tom's ascent lands as dark comedy; the kids' individual endings as tragedy. 97% RT.

episode_reviews.title: The Munsters
episode_reviews.review_body: The final season opens at a party - the siblings together for the first time in apparent solidarity against Logan's GoJo deal, performing the kind of familial warmth the show has spent three seasons establishing they cannot sustain. Jesse Armstrong's writing here is architectural: everything planted in 'The Munsters' will bear weight later, but the planting is disguised as social comedy about people who are awful at being human. Brian Cox's Logan appears briefly and controls every room he enters anyway. The siblings' alliance has the texture of something real and the structural integrity of tissue paper - the episode knows this even if they don't. Jeremy Strong, Kieran Culkin, and Sarah Snook are operating on the specific frequency the show developed over three seasons: saying important things through the form of saying nothing important. The premiere's restraint is correct. The season has one of the great gut-punch episodes in television history coming in episode 3; this episode earns it by letting the audience believe the family dynamic might finally stabilise.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The final season premiere re-establishes the Roy siblings in opposition to Logan's GoJo deal. The family's irreducible dysfunction is immediately back at full voltage. The episode plants the seeds for everything that follows with the show's characteristic precision disguised as chaos.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The Roy siblings' phone conversation - a masterclass in saying nothing while communicating everything.

episode_reviews.title: Connor's Wedding
episode_reviews.review_body: Logan Roy dies in 'Connor's Wedding' - not in a climactic confrontation, not in a hospital bed surrounded by family in a moment of engineered pathos, but off-screen, on a plane, while his three youngest children are attending Connor's wedding. The news arrives by phone. The episode then does something almost impossibly difficult: it holds the camera on Kendall, Shiv, and Roman processing this information in real time, and the result is among the most discussed sequences in prestige television this decade. Jeremy Strong, Sarah Snook, and Kieran Culkin each find separate, credible registers of grief complicated by the specific relationship they each had with their father - grief that is also relief, also horror at the grief, also performance for each other. Roman's breakdown is the most visceral; Shiv's paralysis the most psychologically complex; Kendall's attempt to take charge the most telling about who this man has always been and always been trying not to be. The episode is formally adventurous: director Mark Mylod holds long takes and lets silence do structural work. The comedy of Connor's wedding continuing around the siblings' devastation is not played for laughs - it's played for the precise uncomfortable truth that life doesn't pause. The New York Times called it one of the greatest individual episodes of television ever made. That assessment holds.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Logan Roy dies. Not in a battle or a confrontation - on a plane, out of frame, while his children receive the news by phone at Connor's wedding. The episode is among the most discussed pieces of prestige television in years: grief, comedy, and horror operating simultaneously.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Kendall, Shiv, and Roman on the phone with Frank, trying to process in real time - three performers doing career-best work in a single uncut sequence.

critic_note.text: Connor's Wedding is one of the greatest individual episodes of television ever made.

episode_reviews.title: Church and State
episode_reviews.review_body: 'Church and State' holds two enormous narrative events - Logan Roy's funeral and a presidential election result - and structures them not as parallel plots but as one continuous inquiry into what power means after the man who defined it for everyone in this world is gone. The funeral sequences are the most formally precise writing Succession has produced: each sibling's eulogy is a compressed psychological portrait of their relationship with Logan, their relationship with grief, and their relationship with the performance of grief in public. Shiv's inability to cry, Roman's eulogy collapsing into breakdown, Kendall's managerial attempt to take ownership of the narrative - all three are correct and all three are devastating in different registers. The election result running alongside the funeral is not a distraction; it is the show's argument about the relationship between personal and institutional power, about how Logan-shaped systems outlast Logan. Director Mark Mylod shoots the church with the spatial intelligence of a Kubrick interior - scale used to make humans small. The Guardian's review called it 'flawless television' and the show's penultimate episode is exactly that: a piece of writing and direction confident enough in its accumulated weight to let the grief land at full force without manipulation.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Logan's funeral and the election. Two narrative lines that the show has earned over four seasons reach a convergence point. The eulogies - what each sibling chooses to say about their father - are the most precise writing in the show's run.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Roman's eulogy disintegrating in real time - grief breaking through performance in front of the entire world.

critic_note.text: Church and State is flawless television - Succession at its most devastating and most true.

episode_reviews.title: With Open Eyes
episode_reviews.review_body: The Succession finale divides audiences on first watch and tends to reveal its intelligence on the second. 'With Open Eyes' resolves the succession question with the only honest answer the show's premise ever permitted: the Roy children were never going to inherit their father's empire because the empire was never actually about inheritance. The board vote sequence is constructed as classic dramatic irony - the audience understands the structural logic before each character does. What Shiv does - and the precise, terrible reason she does it - is the most complex moment the show has written for her: a betrayal, a grief response, a power calculation, and an act of self-destruction operating as a single gesture. Tom's elevation lands as dark comedy and as the show's thesis statement about who corporate power actually rewards. The final sequence of each sibling alone - Kendall on the street, Roman at a bar, Shiv in a car with a man she does not love - is filmed with the restraint of a director (Mark Mylod) who trusts the accumulated weight of 39 episodes. The episode was divisive for audiences expecting conventional catharsis. The RT consensus called it the only ending consistent with what the show was always saying. That reading is correct. Succession is one of the two or three best American drama series of the 2010s-2020s, and this finale is entirely worthy of what preceded it.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale: a board vote, three siblings, and an ending that the show earned across every episode. The resolution is not triumphant for anyone. The final image of each Roy sibling is the show's statement about wealth, power, and the thing that was never on offer.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The vote and its aftermath - what Shiv does, what it costs, and the last shot of Kendall alone.

critic_note.text: With Open Eyes ends Succession exactly as it lived: with cruelty, wit, and genuine heartbreak.

seasons.season_over_season: The season the show was always building toward - Logan's absence makes every prior scene retroactively about loss, and the writing honours that.
